title: FAA to finally ditch floppy disks in what it calls "historic" tech upgrade
gist: The FAA will replace 1980s-90s floppy-disk and MS-DOS based air traffic information display systems with Leidos' Enterprise Information Display System (E-IDS) at 435 facilities by end-2028, a project six-plus years in the making under the NextGen program. GAO and DOT reports describe the legacy systems as obsolete and cumbersome for controllers.

insights.claim: The FAA's new Enterprise Information Display System (E-IDS) will be installed in 435 air traffic facilities, replacing several information display systems dating to the 1980s.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: A large federal ATC IT deployment with a defined scope benefits the prime contractor and signals modernization budget flowing.
insights.locator: The FAA said yesterday that it will stop

insights.claim: The FAA plans to complete the E-IDS upgrade at all 435 sites by the end of 2028, with first deployments at Atlantic City, Nashville, Greater Rochester airports and data hubs in Atlanta and Salt Lake City.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Rollout timeline provides milestones for tracking contractor execution and ATC modernization progress.

insights.claim: Leidos was awarded the contract to design and develop E-IDS in August 2020 as part of the FAA's NextGen modernization effort, which encompasses upgrades going back to 2008.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Leidos is the named beneficiary of the deployment phase of a multi-year federal ATC program.

insights.claim: E-IDS replaces IDS-4, ACE-IDS, NIDS and ERIDS; IDS-4 runs on MS-DOS and has been in constant use since the early 1990s on PCs with 3.5-inch floppy drives.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Illustrates the depth of technical debt in critical US infrastructure and the size of the replacement opportunity.
insights.locator: IDS-4, one of the systems being replaced

insights.claim: The FAA says E-IDS addresses two of its top safety concerns: distribution of pilot weather reports (PIREP) and timely distribution of Notices to Airmen (NOTAM).
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Ties the IT spend to aviation safety, making it politically durable across administrations.
insights.locator: The FAA said E-IDS will replace older tools

insights.claim: A September 2026 GAO report said legacy display systems rely on floppy disks, 1980s interfaces, inefficient data organization and manual updates, making them cumbersome for controllers.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Independent oversight confirms the modernization need, supporting continued appropriations.
insights.quote: Legacy display systems rely on obsolete technology (e.g., floppy disks) and interfaces from the 1980s, inefficient data organization, and manual update methods

insights.claim: An April 2026 DOT report said E-IDS will consolidate weather, NOTAMs and airport status into a single view so controllers no longer have to search for information.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Consolidation of fragmented systems lowers sustainment costs as well as improving controller workflow.

insights.claim: Although Trump officials such as Sean Duffy credited the president, the E-IDS plan was shepherded through by officials in both the Biden and Trump administrations.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: ATC modernization is bipartisan, reducing political risk to the program and its contractors.
